set1.q: Which examination findings characterize a healthy hemodialysis fistula?
opts: Faint thrill with no bruit
A missing bruit means the fistula is not healthy and needs referral. A healthy one has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit.
Tender cord with overlying warmth
A tender, warm cord along a vein is superficial thrombophlebitis. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit.
Cool skin and absent pulses
Cool skin with absent pulses suggests ischemia, a complication of a fistula. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit.
Diffuse thrill and soft bruit
Correct. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill you can palpate and a soft bruit you can hear, both with systolic and diastolic components, and it collapses with arm elevation.

set1.q: Which surgery for chronic venous insufficiency is occasionally successful yet has a high rate of postoperative deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Valvuloplasty
Correct. Valvuloplasty is occasionally successful but the incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis is high; the surgical goal is to occlude or remove affected vessels and restore proper flow.
Venous bypass
Venous bypass is described as successful in select patients. The operation with a high postoperative deep vein thrombosis rate is valvuloplasty.
Vein stripping
Vein stripping is a surgical reflux treatment for varicose veins. The chronic venous insufficiency operation with a high postoperative thrombosis rate is valvuloplasty.
Injection sclerotherapy
Sclerotherapy injects a sclerosing agent to obliterate varicose veins and is not a chronic venous insufficiency operation. Valvuloplasty carries the high postoperative thrombosis rate.

set1.q: How is a congenital arteriovenous fistula usually managed?
opts: Conservatively, with elastic support hose
Correct. Congenital fistulas are difficult to treat because the communications can be numerous, so they are treated conservatively with elastic support hose.
Excision of its single communication
Congenital fistulas typically have numerous communications, so a single operation does not close them. Conservative management with elastic support hose is used.
Lifelong anticoagulation
Anticoagulation treats venous thromboembolism, not a fistula. A congenital fistula is managed conservatively with elastic support hose.
Thrombolysis with a filter
Thrombolysis and a vena cava filter address clot. A congenital fistula, with its numerous communications, is treated conservatively with elastic support hose.

set1.q: Which drug class commonly causes bilateral leg swelling without signs of inflammation?
opts: Loop diuretics
Loop diuretics remove fluid and relieve edema. Bilateral swelling without inflammation is typical of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
Calcium channel blockers
Correct. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause drug-induced edema, which is often bilateral and usually lacks any sign of inflammation.
Low molecular weight heparins
Heparins treat clots and do not cause leg edema. Drug-induced swelling is typically from dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
Direct factor Xa inhibitors
These anticoagulants treat clots; their main risk is bleeding, not swelling. Bilateral edema is typical of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

set1.q: What is the gold standard test to confirm superficial thrombophlebitis?
opts: Computed tomography angiography
Computed tomography angiography is used to confirm and map an arteriovenous fistula. Superficial thrombophlebitis is confirmed by venous duplex ultrasound.
Venous duplex ultrasound
Correct. Diagnosis is based on history and examination and is confirmed by venous duplex ultrasound, the gold standard, which shows a noncompressible superficial vein with clot and a thickened wall.
D-dimer measurement
A D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, showing only fibrinolysis somewhere. Superficial thrombophlebitis is confirmed by venous duplex ultrasound of the vein.
Contrast ascending venography
Venography was the older reference test for deep vein thrombosis and has been replaced by ultrasound. Superficial thrombophlebitis is confirmed by venous duplex ultrasound.

set1.q: Which finding is most sensitive for a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Leg warmth
Warmth is 72% sensitive, the lowest of the three quoted findings. Swelling, at 97%, is the most sensitive.
A positive Homan sign
The Homan sign (calf pain when the foot is flexed upward) is neither sensitive nor specific. Leg swelling, at 97% sensitive, is the most sensitive finding.
Leg swelling
Correct. Leg swelling is 97% sensitive, ahead of leg pain (86%) and warmth (72%); its high sensitivity makes it the finding most often present.
Leg pain
Pain is 86% sensitive, common but less so than swelling at 97%. Swelling is the most sensitive finding.

set1.q: What is the mainstay of treatment for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Anticoagulation
Correct. Anticoagulation is the mainstay of treatment; some patients also need thrombolysis or lifelong anticoagulation, depending on the situation.
Thrombolysis
Thrombolysis, which breaks down the clot, is added for selected patients such as large proximal clots. The mainstay for everyone is anticoagulation.
Inferior vena cava filter
A filter is reserved for proximal clot when anticoagulation cannot be given. The mainstay of treatment is anticoagulation.
Thrombectomy
Thrombectomy is a procedure for selected large clots. The mainstay of treatment for deep vein thrombosis is anticoagulation.

set1.q: Which oral agent may help accelerate healing of venous ulcers?
opts: Furosemide
A loop diuretic does not improve venous ulcer healing, and venous edema is controlled with compression. Aspirin may help accelerate healing.
Warfarin
Anticoagulation treats and prevents clots but does not speed venous ulcer healing. Aspirin is the oral agent that may help accelerate healing.
Aspirin
Correct. Aspirin may help accelerate venous ulcer healing, though no oral medication has been proven useful for treating venous disease; flavonoids are used to increase venous tone.
Prednisone
Oral corticosteroids are not used to heal venous ulcers and can impair wound healing. Aspirin may help, and flavonoids increase venous tone.

set1.q: How long is anticoagulation given after a venous thromboembolism provoked by a minor transient risk factor?
opts: 6 to 12 months
Twelve months exceeds the range given. A minor transient risk factor is treated for 3 to 6 months.
An indefinite period
An indefinite course is for unprovoked clots with no identifiable risk factor. A minor transient risk factor is treated for 3 to 6 months.
3 to 6 months
Correct. Minor transient risk factors, such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel or minor leg injury, are treated for 3 to 6 months.
3 months exactly
Three months is the duration for a major transient risk factor. A minor one is treated for 3 to 6 months.

set1.q: Why can a positive D-dimer not confirm deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Many conditions raise it
Correct. A positive D-dimer means fibrinolysis is occurring somewhere in the body, which many conditions cause, so imaging is needed to show a clot in the leg veins.
It is often falsely negative
A negative result is reassuring, since the test is sensitive. The problem is that a positive result is nonspecific.
It detects only arterial clots
D-dimer marks fibrin breakdown in any vascular bed. It cannot confirm a venous clot because many conditions raise it.
It shows the clot location
D-dimer is a blood test and cannot show a location. It cannot confirm a clot because many conditions raise it.

set1.q: Which chronic complication follows deep vein thrombosis 6 to 24 months later?
opts: Post-thrombotic syndrome
Correct. Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis, appearing from 6 to 24 months afterward.
Lymphedema
Lymphedema usually follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation. The complication of a prior clot is post-thrombotic syndrome.
Arteriovenous fistula
An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal artery to vein connection. The delayed complication of a clot is post-thrombotic syndrome.
Superficial thrombophlebitis
Superficial thrombophlebitis is inflammation with a clot in a surface vein, not a delayed sequel. The delayed complication of a deep clot is post-thrombotic syndrome.

set1.q: What is first-line management of uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis?
opts: Inferior vena cava filter
A filter is for acute proximal leg deep vein thrombosis when anticoagulation is contraindicated. Superficial thrombophlebitis rarely embolizes and is treated with warmth and anti-inflammatories.
Anticoagulation for three months
Anticoagulation is added only for extensive clot or intermediate or higher thrombosis risk. A minimum of three months is the deep vein thrombosis course, not first-line here.
Warm compresses and ibuprofen
Correct. Typical treatment is warm compresses, compression and elevation of the limb, with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen or diclofenac for pain and inflammation.
Thrombolysis with alteplase
Thrombolysis is reserved for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism with stable blood pressure. Superficial thrombophlebitis uses warm compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug.

set1.q: Andexanet alfa is the reversal agent for which pair of anticoagulants?
opts: Fondaparinux and dabigatran
Neither is reversed by andexanet alfa. It reverses the direct factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Apixaban and rivaroxaban
Correct. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban, the direct factor Xa inhibitors, and its use is off-label for edoxaban as well.
Dabigatran and warfarin
Dabigatran is reversed by idarucizumab and warfarin by prothrombin complex concentrate. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Heparin and enoxaparin
Heparins are reversed by protamine sulfate. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.

set1.q: Which is a risk factor for chronic venous disease?
opts: Ligamentous laxity (flat feet)

Correct. Ligamentous laxity, for example flat feet, is a listed risk factor, along with advancing age, female sex, family history, higher body mass index, smoking, prior thrombosis and high estrogen states.
Male sex
Female sex is the listed risk factor, along with higher parity and high estrogen states. Being male does not raise the risk of chronic venous disease in the way female sex does.
Lower body mass index
An increased body mass index raises risk, not a lower one. Extra weight adds to venous pressure in the legs, so a lower index is not a risk factor for chronic venous disease.
Regular calf muscle exercise
Calf exercise helps the muscle pump move blood upward, and inadequate pump function is itself a cause of venous hypertension. Regular exercise is protective, not a risk factor.

set1.q: Which study is the gold standard for diagnosing deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Plasma D-dimer
D-dimer is a sensitive rule-out test but not specific. The gold standard is contrast ascending venography.
Magnetic resonance venography
Magnetic resonance is an option when ultrasound is nondiagnostic. The definitive gold standard is contrast ascending venography.
Contrast ascending venography
Correct. Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard, but because it is invasive and needs injected dye it has been replaced in practice by ultrasound.
Venous duplex ultrasound
Ultrasound is the test used in practice, having replaced venography. The gold standard remains contrast ascending venography.

set1.q: What is the most common predisposing factor for varicose veins?
opts: Pregnancy
Women after pregnancy are at increased risk, but this is not the most common predisposing factor. Family history takes that position.
Family history
Correct. Family history is the most common predisposing factor for developing varicose veins; periods of high venous pressure and pregnancy also contribute.
Prolonged standing
Prolonged standing raises venous pressure and is a risk factor, but it is not the most common one. Family history is the most common predisposing factor.
Heavy lifting
Heavy lifting causes high venous pressure and is a risk factor, though not the most common. Family history is the most common predisposing factor.

set1.q: Where does the itching of chronic venous disease often begin?
opts: Around the lateral malleolus
The outer ankle is where arterial insufficiency ulcers tend to sit. Venous itching typically begins around the medial malleolus, the inner ankle, before spreading up the lower leg.
Over the dorsum of the foot
The top of the foot is not the usual starting site. Itching from venous hypertension typically begins around the medial malleolus, the bony prominence on the inner ankle.
Behind the knee in the popliteal fossa
The popliteal fossa is not where venous itch starts. Pruritus of chronic venous disease usually begins at the inner ankle, around the medial malleolus, where venous pressure changes show first.
Around the medial malleolus
Correct. Itching of the lower legs often starts around the medial malleolus, the inner ankle; arterial disease tends to affect the lateral side, so a medial start points toward a venous cause.

set1.q: In adults, above what age does age become a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: 60 years
Correct. Age above 60 years is listed among the other risk factors for deep vein thrombosis, alongside overweight, heart failure, cancer, chronic kidney disease and a sedentary lifestyle.
40 years
Forty is younger than the listed threshold. Age becomes a listed risk factor above 60 years.
50 years
Fifty is below the stated threshold. Age is listed as a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis above 60 years.
75 years
Seventy-five is later than the stated threshold. Age is listed as a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis above 60 years.

opts: That range describes lower extremity clots, which embolize far more often. For upper extremity clots the figure is only up to 6%.
Nearly half is well above any figure given for either limb. Upper extremity clots embolize in up to 6%, lower extremity clots in 15% to 30%.
Almost never
Embolism is uncommon in the arm but not absent. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper extremity clots, against 15% to 30% for the leg.
Up to 6%
Correct. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper extremity clots, compared with 15% to 30% of lower extremity clots, so the leg carries far greater embolic risk.

set1.q: What is the primary presenting symptom of chronic venous insufficiency?
opts: Cool, pale toes
Cool pale toes signal arterial insufficiency. In chronic venous insufficiency the limb is swollen, and the primary presenting symptom is progressive pitting edema.
Numbness across the foot
Numbness suggests neuropathy rather than venous disease. The primary presenting symptom of chronic venous insufficiency is progressive pitting edema, with discomfort on standing.
Progressive pitting edema
Correct. Progressive pitting edema of the leg, usually the lower leg, is the primary presenting symptom, typically with dull discomfort that worsens on standing.
Calf pain when walking
Pain on walking that eases with rest is claudication from arterial disease. Chronic venous insufficiency presents mainly with progressive pitting edema of the lower leg.

set1.q: What defines superficial phlebitis?
opts: Vein wall inflammation without a clot

Correct. Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the wall of a vein in the absence of thrombus; when a clot is also present the condition is called superficial thrombophlebitis and is treated differently.
Vein wall inflammation with a clot
That describes superficial thrombophlebitis. Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall with no thrombus, and the presence of a clot is what changes the name.
Infected vein wall with pus
Pus, high fever and fluctuance point to septic (suppurative) thrombophlebitis. Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall without a clot and without signs of infection.
Clot within a deep leg vein
That describes deep vein thrombosis, clot formation in the deep veins, usually of the legs. Superficial phlebitis involves the wall of a superficial vein, with no thrombus.

set1.q: Under the Virchow triad, cancer belongs to which component?
opts: Venous stasis
The stasis component covers immobilization, venous insufficiency and heart failure. Cancer makes blood clot more readily, a hypercoagulable state.
Endothelial trauma
Endothelial trauma covers surgery, trauma, burns and injected drug use. Cancer is a hypercoagulable state in the Virchow triad.
None of the three
Cancer is listed under the triad. It belongs to the hypercoagulable state, together with oral contraceptives and pregnancy.
Hypercoagulable state
Correct. Cancer sits in the hypercoagulable component of the Virchow triad, alongside oral contraceptives, postmenopausal estrogen therapy and pregnancy, all of which tip blood toward clotting.

set1.q: For how long after delivery does postpartum status raise deep vein thrombosis risk?
opts: The first 6 to 12 weeks
Correct. The first 6 to 12 weeks postpartum is a listed risk factor for deep vein thrombosis, and pregnancy itself adds a hypercoagulable state and pelvic vein involvement.
The first 2 weeks only
Two weeks is too short. The listed risk period is the first 6 to 12 weeks after delivery.
The first 6 months
Six months overshoots the listed window. The listed period of raised risk is the first 6 to 12 weeks postpartum.
The first 2 years
Two years is far longer than the listed window. Risk is raised through the first 6 to 12 weeks after delivery.

set1.q: What is the purpose of emollients in venous skin care?
opts: Shrink the dilated veins
Emollients act on the skin surface only. Dilated veins are compressed by hosiery or bandages; emollients maintain the skin barrier and prevent fissuring.
Dissolve deeper skin scarring
Scarring of skin and fat in lipodermatosclerosis is not dissolved by a moisturizer. Emollients maintain the skin barrier, preventing dryness and fissuring.
Prevent new clot formation
Skin care does not affect coagulation. Emollients maintain the skin barrier and reduce scratching; compression and mobility address venous stasis.
Maintain the skin barrier
Correct. Emollients maintain the skin barrier, preventing dryness and fissuring and reducing scratching, which lowers the risk of skin breakdown in chronic venous insufficiency.

set1.q: How is an arteriovenous fistula of the extremity diagnosed?
opts: By skin punch biopsy
A punch biopsy helps sort out the causes of leg ulcers when the diagnosis is uncertain. A fistula is diagnosed by physical examination.
By ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index screens for peripheral artery disease, not fistulas. An arteriovenous fistula is diagnosed by physical examination.
By physical examination
Correct. Diagnosis is determined by physical examination; computed tomography angiography and angiography can then confirm it and give the location and size of the fistula.
By D-dimer measurement
A D-dimer reflects fibrinolysis and is used to rule out venous thromboembolism. A fistula is diagnosed by physical examination, then confirmed with imaging.

set1.q: Which inherited hypercoagulable state is listed among the Virchow triad risk factors?
opts: Estrogen replacement
Postmenopausal estrogen therapy is acquired. Inherited hypercoagulable states include factor V Leiden and the protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiencies.
Factor V Leiden
Correct. Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited hypercoagulable state and heads the list, which also names prothrombin gene mutation and protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiency.
Cancer
Cancer is a hypercoagulable state but an acquired one. Inherited examples include factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation and protein C or S deficiency.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy is an acquired hypercoagulable state. Inherited examples are factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation and protein C, S or antithrombin deficiency.

set1.q: Where should a patient with a venous ulcer be referred for care?
opts: A pain management clinic
Pain clinics do not heal ulcers. A venous ulcer heals only with edema control and compression, delivered through wound care management.
Wound care management
Correct. Venous ulcers are referred to wound care management, because they will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied, and healing can take months.
A hematology clinic
Hematology addresses clotting disorders. A venous ulcer needs wound care management, with edema control and compression, and usually months of healing.
A rheumatology clinic
Rheumatology manages autoimmune disease, one of the causes considered when an ulcer is unclear. A venous ulcer is referred to wound care management.

set1.q: For superficial thrombophlebitis, which situation prompts adding anticoagulation?
opts: Pain relieved by warm compresses
Relief with warm compresses means the usual treatment is working. Anticoagulation is added for extensive clot burden or higher thrombosis risk.
Extensive clot or higher thrombosis risk
Correct. Anticoagulation may be started when clot burden is extensive or the patient is at intermediate or higher risk of thrombosis; otherwise warm compresses and anti-inflammatories are enough.
Any tender palpable cord in a leg
A tender cord is the ordinary presentation and is managed with warm compresses and anti-inflammatories. Anticoagulation is for extensive clot or higher thrombosis risk.
Purulent drainage over the vein
Purulent drainage suggests infection within the vein, which is septic thrombophlebitis. The trigger for anticoagulation is extensive clot or higher thrombosis risk.

set1.q: How is the D-dimer characterized as a test for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: Both sensitive and specific
A test that is both would confirm the diagnosis alone. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result needs ultrasound.
Neither sensitive nor specific
That describes the Homan sign, not D-dimer. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific.
Sensitive but not specific
Correct. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: a negative result is reassuring, while a positive result may reflect fibrinolysis from many causes rather than a deep vein thrombosis.
Specific but not sensitive
The reverse is true. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so it detects most clots yet is often raised without one.

set1.q: In the low likelihood Wells category, what happens after a negative D-dimer?
opts: The test is repeated in a week
Repeat imaging applies after a negative ultrasound in high likelihood patients. A negative D-dimer in the low category ends the work-up.
The work-up stops
Correct. In the low likelihood Wells category a negative D-dimer ends the work-up, since the test is sensitive enough to rule out deep vein thrombosis.
Duplex ultrasound follows
Ultrasound follows a positive D-dimer, not a negative one. A negative result in the low likelihood category ends the work-up.
Venography is performed
Venography is invasive and largely replaced by ultrasound. A negative D-dimer in the low category ends the work-up.

set2.q: After a negative thigh ultrasound in the high likelihood Wells category, which option is listed?
opts: Repeat thigh ultrasound in a week
Correct. A negative thigh ultrasound in a high likelihood patient does not end the work-up: lower leg ultrasound, phlebography or a repeat thigh ultrasound in a week can follow.
Discharge with no follow-up
High pretest probability means a single negative ultrasound is not enough. Further imaging, such as a repeat thigh ultrasound in a week, follows.
Immediate thrombolysis
Thrombolysis treats a confirmed large clot. After a negative ultrasound, lower leg ultrasound, phlebography or repeat ultrasound follows.
Inferior vena cava filter placement
A filter is for confirmed proximal clot with contraindication to anticoagulation. After a negative ultrasound, more imaging follows.

set2.q: What share of all deep vein thromboses occur in the upper extremity?
opts: Correct. Upper extremity clots make up only 5% to 10% of all deep vein thromboses, although the incidence is rising each year; the lower extremity accounts for the great majority.
One in four is far too high. Upper extremity clots are only 5% to 10% of the total, and lower extremity clots are about ten times more common.
Half would make the arm as common as the leg. The upper extremity accounts for only 5% to 10% of deep vein thromboses; the leg carries the rest.
Under 1%
Under 1% understates it. Upper extremity clots are uncommon but make up 5% to 10% of all deep vein thromboses, and their incidence is rising annually.
